content.title: About
content.content: Bread is a staple food made by baking dough from flour, water, yeast and salt. Egg is the nutrient‑rich reproductive part of birds, widely used in cooking. Challah is a traditional Jewish braided loaf, prepared from a yeasted dough enriched with eggs, oil and sometimes honey.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bread has been made for over 10,000 years; the earliest forms were simple flatbreads baked on open fires.
Eggs are an almost perfect protein source, containing all essential amino acids in optimal ratios.
Challah is traditionally baked for Shabbat and holidays; its braiding symbolizes the intertwining of family bonds.
In many cultures bread is a symbol of life and prosperity, and a slice of bread is often used in greeting rituals.
Unwashed eggs can be stored in the refrigerator for up to 5 weeks.

items.title: Energy supply
items.content: Bread and challah provide quick‑release carbohydrates, while eggs deliver high‑quality protein for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Whole‑grain bread and eggs are rich in B1, B2, B6 and B12 vitamins, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Eggs contain iron, phosphorus and selenium; challah often gains extra calcium and magnesium from added dairy.

items.title: Choline
items.content: Eggs are one of the best dietary sources of choline, essential for brain health and liver function.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain bread and challah made with whole‑meal flour supply dietary fiber that aids regular digestion.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals develop an allergy to egg white proteins, which can cause skin reactions up to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Gluten in bread
items.content: Wheat‑based bread contains gluten, which may cause problems for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Commercial breads often contain high levels of salt; excess sodium can raise blood pressure.

items.title: Cholesterol
items.content: Egg yolks contain cholesterol; those with elevated cholesterol levels should moderate egg intake.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Raw or undercooked eggs can harbor Salmonella; it is important to cook eggs thoroughly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Bread can be eaten fresh, toasted, as sandwiches, or used in soups and casseroles. Eggs are boiled, fried, made into omelets, pâtés and incorporated into baked goods. Challah is served as a festive loaf, often sliced and spread with butter or honey.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store bread and challah in a paper bag or bread box at room temperature for up to 3 days; for longer storage keep them in a sealed container in the refrigerator (up to 7 days). Keep eggs in their original carton in the fridge, where they stay fresh for up to 5 weeks.

content.title: About
content.content: Pickled radishes are fresh radish roots that have been fermented or brined in a vinegar solution with salt, sugar, spices, and sometimes aromatic herbs. They retain a crisp texture and develop a tangy‑sweet flavor typical of many snack foods.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Radishes belong to the Brassicaceae family, making them relatives of cabbage, broccoli, and mustard.
Pickling extends the shelf life of radishes, allowing storage in the refrigerator for several months.
Different cultures have distinct recipes: Japan often uses rice vinegar and sea salt, while Russia commonly adds mustard seeds and dill.
The bright pink color of some pickled radishes can be enhanced with beet juice or food coloring.
Radishes are rich in vitamin C, which remains partially intact after pickling.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Low‑calorie snack
items.content: Radishes are low in calories, making them suitable for weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Phytonutrients in radishes help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports heart health
items.content: Low sodium in homemade brine and the presence of potassium contribute to normal blood pressure.

items.title: Allergy to cruciferous vegetables
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to radishes.

items.title: Salt content
items.content: Pickling brine can be salty; people limiting sodium should monitor portion size.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Improper storage can lead to growth of harmful bacteria. Keep refrigerated and respect the use‑by date.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pickled radishes are served as a snack, added to salads, sandwiches, sushi rolls, vegetarian wraps, or used as a garnish for meat dishes. They can be eaten straight from the jar.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the jar of pickled radishes in the refrigerator at 0 °C–4 °C. After opening, consume within 2–3 weeks. Discard if an off‑odor or mold appears.

yogurt-greek-whole-milk-fruit.title: Greek Yogurt with Whole Milk and Fruit

content.title: About
content.content: Greek yogurt made from whole milk with fruit additions is a thick, creamy dairy product created by straining regular yogurt. It is rich in protein, calcium, and probiotics, while the fruit provides natural sweetness and a boost of vitamins.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Greek yogurt contains two to three times more protein than regular yogurt.
Traditional straining removes most of the whey, giving it a dense texture.
Fruit mixes often use seasonal berries and fruits, increasing vitamin C content.
In Greece, yogurt is a national staple and is frequently served with honey and nuts.
Probiotics in yogurt support gut health and boost immunity.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: Protein supports muscle growth and repair and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: Calcium strengthens bones and teeth, while vitamin D enhances its absorption.

items.title: Probiotics
items.content: Beneficial bacteria promote a healthy gut microbiome and may improve digestion.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Yogurt provides vitamin B12 and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants from fruit
items.content: Fruit adds vitamin C and polyphenols that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Although some lactose is removed during straining, the product still contains it.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People allergic to casein or whey may react to Greek yogurt.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Fruit sweeteners can raise sugar levels, especially in flavored varieties.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Whole‑milk Greek yogurt is more calorie‑dense than low‑fat versions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy it as a snack, blend into smoothies, use in sauces, desserts, or as a base for dressings. Fruit pieces make it a tasty breakfast with granola or nuts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the yogurt in the refrigerator at 1‑4 °C. Once opened, consume within 5‑7 days and do not leave at room temperature for more than 2 hours.
